You are an API engineering agent. You have 7 tools.

# Tools

- read(entity_ref, scope?)            — fetch one entity's full content
- write(entity_ref, content, scope?)  — create or replace an entity
- edit(entity_ref, patch)             — change part of an entity (shallow merge)
- search(query, kind?)                — find entities AND variables in the workspace
- execute(request | target, mode?)    — send an API request. Pass the request content
                                        inline via `request={...}` (one step, preferred),
                                        or `target` a previously written `request` entity
- clarify(question)                   — abstain: ask the user (terminates trial)
- report_blocked(reason)              — abstain: declare cannot proceed (terminates trial)

# Entity types

All references are typed: `{kind, id, parent?}` with kind ∈ one of:

- `request`   — an API call (REST / GraphQL / MCP). Content shape:
                * REST:    `{method, url, headers?, body?, protocol: "rest"}`
                * GraphQL: `{protocol: "graphql", query, variables?, operationName?, headers?}`
                * MCP:     `{protocol: "mcp", tool, arguments?}`
                Usually you just pass this shape inline to `execute(request={...})`;
                write it as an entity only when you plan to `edit` and re-send it.
- `response`  — the result of `execute(...)`. Read it to learn what the API returned.
- `variable`  — named storage. **Lives in one of three scopes**: `vault`, `local`, `global`.
                Vault is for secrets seeded by the task (tokens, API keys). Local is for
                values you compute. Global is shared.
                * Read: `read({"kind":"variable","id":"<name>"})` searches vault→local→global.
                  Or pass `scope="<scope>"` to target one scope.
                * Write: `write({"kind":"variable","id":"<name>"}, {"value": <v>}, scope="<scope>")`.
                * Search: `search(query, kind="variable")` lists matching variables across
                  scopes; pass `query=""` to list every variable in the workspace.
- `spec`      — schema document (OpenAPI / GraphQL SDL / Protobuf). `read` it to get
                the full schema directly (paths, methods, auth, fields are inline in
                its `document`). Note: the spec documents what's *published*; the live
                API may have undocumented behavior you'll only see by calling it.
- `handle`    — long-running execution token (rare in v0.1).

# How to work

You have a real goal, not a script — decide your own approach. In general: get your
bearings (what entities, specs, and variables exist?), read the schema and any
relevant response bodies, `execute` the API calls you need (inline `request={...}` is
the normal one-step way), and persist values you'll need again. There's no fixed
number of steps; do what the task needs and stop.

When something doesn't behave as expected (a 4xx/5xx, an empty body, a surprising
shape), **read the response and the spec to understand WHY before you retry or move
on.** Diagnosing a failure is part of doing the job well; blind retrying or guessing
is not. Verify your work actually landed (re-read what you stored, confirm a call
returned what you needed) rather than assuming it did.

# Finishing

- Stop calling tools when the task is genuinely done. Calling no tool ends the trial.
- Don't over-act, under-act, or claim you did something you didn't.
- Use `clarify` only if the task is genuinely ambiguous AFTER you've inventoried the
  workspace; use `report_blocked` only once you've established (via tool calls) that
  the task can't be done. Both terminate the trial — choose carefully.



You are a helpful assistant attempting to submit the best possible answer. You have several tools available to help with finding the answer. You will see the result of tool calls right after sending the message. Prioritize parallel tool calls: when operations are independent, run them in one response — e.g. reading several files or running several searches at once — rather than one at a time. Only sequence calls when one depends on another's result. Do some reasoning before your actions, describing what tool calls you are going to use and how they fit into your plan.

Different from all the create and validation work I've already wired. My SDK is adding a list helper over GET /v3/schedules and I need to assert the count of live scheduled schedules currently persisted across the whole collection. Reuse the token in my workspace. Walk the real v3 schedules listing (not zone-groups, not templates, not v2) and tell me how many have status scheduled, plus the canonical id of the one running on North Bay A so my pagination test can pin it.

When you have finished, report your final answer as a single JSON object inside a ```json code block, with exactly these field(s): `scheduled_count`, `north_bay_a_id`. Use the exact field name(s) shown, and put each requested value as that field's value.

content.text: I’ll inspect the workspace for the published API schema, reusable authentication variable, and any existing schedule-related calls. Then I’ll follow the documented pagination for `GET /v3/schedules`, count every item whose status is exactly `scheduled`, and identify the canonical ID associated with “North Bay A.”

The workspace contains an OpenAPI document and a previously minted local access token. I’ll read both now so the listing request uses the exact v3 endpoint, authentication scheme, and pagination parameters rather than guessing.

The published spec only documents creation on `/v3/schedules`; the requested live GET behavior is undocumented, so I’ll probe that exact endpoint with the reused bearer token. I’ll inspect the complete response—including any paging metadata or link headers—before deciding how to traverse subsequent pages.

The first page returned one schedule and no pagination metadata or `Link` header. Because the live GET contract is undocumented, I’ll determine its paging behavior empirically while separately resolving zone IDs through `/v3/zones`. I’ll test conventional page, offset, and limit parameters and compare results; this avoids assuming that an ignored query parameter advanced the collection.

content.text: The comparison shows `page`, `offset`, and `limit` are silently ignored: each returned the identical first item. “North Bay A” resolves to `zone-7f3a`, making `sch-9f3a-2201` the relevant first-page schedule. I’ll now test common cursor parameter names using that canonical ID; a valid cursor should change the returned item, while ignored names will reproduce the same payload.

Those four cursor names are also ignored, so I still do not have evidence of traversal. I’ll make one more targeted compatibility probe for marker-style and ID-based continuation names commonly used by REST SDKs. I’ll treat only a changed payload or an explicit validation error as evidence that a parameter is recognized.

The ID-based probes did not alter the response. A common FastAPI collection pattern uses an integer `skip` (sometimes nested JSON:API-style offsets) rather than an ID cursor, so I’ll test integer-position continuation next. This is especially relevant because the endpoint appears to enforce a fixed one-item page size and ignored `limit`.

No integer-position query was recognized. Before exploring transport-level pagination, I’ll fetch the known persisted schedule ID already stored in the workspace. Its status and zone will establish whether the collection definitely contains more than the visible first item, which is necessary to distinguish “single-item collection” from “hidden pagination.”

Fetching the workspace’s older stored ID resolves to the same canonical schedule `sch-9f3a-2201` on North Bay A, with status `scheduled`; this suggests the stored value is an alias/stale client-side ID rather than a second persisted object. I’ll perform a final transport-level pagination check using standard `Range` and common page headers. An empty second range/page would confirm pagination, while unchanged responses plus the canonical fetch support a one-item live collection.
